proposals.name: Prompt-specific causal integration
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story's central conflict, image, or turning point is causally dependent on the specific, distinctive element given in the writing prompt (a named object, rule, or situation), rather than using the prompt as a generic launching pad that is dropped after the opening lines. HIGH: the prompt's distinctive premise actively drives what happens and how it resolves -- remove the premise and the story collapses. LOW: the prompt's specific hook (an object, a rule, a visual detail) is mentioned once near the top and then never influences the plot again; the rest could be pasted onto almost any other prompt.
proposals.rationale: In R01 the prompt is a single evocative word ('Clockwork') but nothing in the tavern/bouncer/hidden-daughter scene engages with clockwork, mechanism, or time at all -- it reads as a stock urban-fantasy episode. In R04 the prompt's specific hook (a statue that blinks) is used only as an opening gag and is never returned to or explained; the rest of the scene is generic stoner banter. Both score very high on the scorecard despite this (R01 0.987, R04 0.970), suggesting the scorecard may not be checking whether a story actually develops its prompt's distinctive premise.

proposals.name: Borrowed vs self-generated emotional weight
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story's emotional or dramatic resonance is generated by the story's own characters, world, and choices, or is substantially imported by inserting an already-famous character/setting (a franchise, myth, or widely known figure) whose pre-existing weight does work the prose itself has not earned. HIGH: any gravity in the piece is built from scratch within the text. LOW: the piece leans on outside recognition of a borrowed character or IP to supply stakes, backstory, or pathos it never dramatizes itself.
proposals.rationale: R09 lifts Dr. Tenma and Tobio directly from Astro Boy, and its emotional pull ('I'm sorry about your son') depends on the reader's outside knowledge of that story rather than anything established in this text; it scores 0.904 on the scorecard despite almost no original characterization. R37 similarly imports Freddy Krueger wholesale and scores 0.980. Contrast R33, which builds an entirely original devotional guard-dog mythology from the ground up and is rated far lower by the scorecard (~0.12) despite arguably doing more original work.

proposals.name: Structure enacts theme, not just states it
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story's formal choices -- repetition, refrain, fragmented syntax, an unusual document/log format, disordered chronology -- are themselves doing thematic work (the form mimics or embodies the content), versus a conventional scene-by-scene telling with no structural relationship to its subject. HIGH: the way the piece is built (its shape, syntax, or format) is inseparable from what it's about. LOW: the story could be told in a completely conventional structure without losing anything essential.
proposals.rationale: R32's fractured, repetitive counting prose ('1, 2, 3. 1, 2, 3... 24. Sorry. 24. Or was it 72?') formally reproduces the disorientation of its time-loop premise. R33 bookends and threads the piece with the ritual refrain 'To serve is the highest honour,' turning repetition into a liturgical structure mirroring the guard-dog's devotion. R34 tells its whole story as escalating timestamped transmission logs, so the format itself is the mystery/reveal mechanism. All three score extremely high with the dense model (0.945-0.998) but very low on the scorecard (roughly 0.115-0.145), suggesting the scorecard isn't crediting structural/formal ambition.

proposals.name: Transgression serves meaning, not shock alone
proposals.instruction: When a story includes violence, gore, or taboo content, judge whether that content is doing ironic or thematic work connected to the story's premise, versus functioning only as shock value or a punchline-delivery mechanism with no further resonance. HIGH: the disturbing content is inseparable from the story's idea -- removing it would remove the point. LOW: the disturbing content could be swapped for any other shock beat without changing what the story is actually about.
proposals.rationale: R06's repeated, escalating gruesome deaths of the same character are the literal embodiment of its prompt (characters resenting an author who 'constantly causes conflict in their lives') -- the violence IS the joke and the theme fused together. R39's body horror (eating alien flesh, losing human squeamishness) is the vehicle for the narrator's moral/identity transformation across the piece. Compare R38, whose graphic torture is a stand-alone slasher shock beat that exists mainly to deliver the prompt's line as a pun, with no thematic development beforehand. R06 and R39 score 0.889 and 0.986 with the dense model, versus R38's 0.087 -- but the scorecard rates R38 highest of the three (0.950).

proposals.name: Individuated psychological interiority
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the point-of-view character's inner experience is rendered with specific, particular detail (a distinct train of thought, a concrete bodily sensation, a specific self-justification) rather than through generic emotional shorthand ('heart pounding,' 'terrified') or dialogue that exists purely to convey plot facts. HIGH: you could not swap this character's interiority into another story without it feeling wrong. LOW: the character's stated emotions are interchangeable stock phrases, or all information arrives through undifferentiated dialogue.
proposals.rationale: R05 renders Cora's specific physical panic (goosebumps, scanning the room, tripping over a body, fighting not to vomit) in granular, embodied detail. R14 gives Mason a particular, ongoing internal rationalization about resenting Kale ('Don't let it bother you... Kale was his friend... It was getting harder by the day'). By contrast R01 relies almost entirely on generic tags ('my heart pounding,' 'dry lips') and R08 is pure undifferentiated banter between two interchangeable bureaucrats with no interior access at all -- yet R01 and R08 score 0.987 and 0.948 on the scorecard against R05/R14's dense scores of 0.954/0.969.

proposals.name: Sustained, distinctive narrating voice
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the narration maintains one deliberate, recognizable register (specific diction, syntax, and tone appropriate to who is narrating) consistently across the whole piece, versus drifting into a flat, generic, or inconsistent register that could belong to any narrator. HIGH: you could identify this piece from a blind paragraph because of its voice. LOW: the prose reads as interchangeable default 'competent internet fiction' voice, or shifts registers without motivation.
proposals.rationale: R19 sustains an ironic, baroque essayistic voice for its entire length ('the dance of the thing,' 'greedy as crows') without breaking register. R22 holds a confident, wry comic voice throughout its demon narration. By contrast R09's dialogue is flat and interchangeable between its two speakers, and R35's exposition-heavy scene-setting uses generic phrasing ('He couldn't believe his eyes') that doesn't individuate its narrator. R19/R22 score 0.924/0.995 with the dense model versus R09/R35's scorecard scores of 0.904/0.863.

proposals.name: Craft investment proportional to length
proposals.instruction: For short pieces especially, judge whether the available space is used to build at least one instance of developed imagery, scene-setting, or a complete idea, versus being a bare sketch or single one-line gag with no descriptive or structural development at all. HIGH: even in a few sentences, the piece does real descriptive or conceptual work. LOW: the piece is essentially a fragment or a shrug -- a setup with nothing built in between.
proposals.rationale: R02 is three sentences long, contains no scene, no image, and no character beyond a single flat joke about bad autobiographical writing. R17 is similarly very short but sustains an actual image-driven conceit (a secret wizard aiding Caesar, da Vinci, and Wozniak across centuries) building to a deliberate closing beat ('I answer the phone'). R02 scores 0.993 on the scorecard -- the single highest scorecard value in this entire slice -- while the dense model rates it 0.182; R17 scores the opposite way (dense 0.921, card 0.128).

proposals.name: Reveal deepens rather than merely closes
proposals.instruction: When a story ends on a twist, reveal, or punchline, judge whether that turn recontextualizes or adds meaning to everything that came before it, versus simply providing mechanical closure or a 'gotcha' whose main function is to end the piece cleverly. HIGH: rereading the story with the ending in mind changes how earlier details land. LOW: the ending is a clean stopping point but doesn't change or deepen anything that preceded it.
proposals.rationale: R10's 'Nelson's my boa!' reveal is a fun capping joke but doesn't retroactively deepen the classroom-chaos anecdote that preceded it. R30's death-announcement-via-texting-slang is a single ironic juxtaposition with no character development before it to be recontextualized. Compare R33, where the alpha's death recontextualizes the entire preceding devotional monologue ('To serve is the highest honour') by testing that devotion against genuine loss. R10 and R30 score 0.911/0.975 on the scorecard; R33 scores roughly 0.12 with the dense model rating it near the top instead.

proposals.name: Concrete sensory specificity
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the prose renders its world through specific, unexpected sensory detail (particular sights, smells, textures, sounds) rather than through abstract statement or generic descriptors that could apply to any scene of the same type. HIGH: at least one image in the piece is genuinely specific and surprising. LOW: description relies on stock phrases ('a chill of recognition,' 'couldn't believe his eyes') that carry no particular sensory information.
proposals.rationale: R07 has images like 'drops of lemon juice raining like bitter little pellets upon his broken skin' -- a specific, invented sensory image. R39's visceral description of the taste of alien flesh is similarly concrete. By contrast R23's fantasy-quest prose relies on generic phrasing ('resonate with some soft glow') and R35's scene uses boilerplate description ('he couldn't believe his eyes'; 'a chill of recognition'). R07/R39 score 0.924/0.986 with the dense model; R23/R35 score 0.951/0.863 on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Diction precision and internal consistency
proposals.instruction: Judge whether word choices are used correctly and consistently, and whether small factual/continuity details (spelling of body parts, repeated invented terms) are handled with control, distinguishing genuine precision from small slips a careful editor would flag. HIGH: word choices are exact and repeatable details stay consistent. LOW: there is a word-choice error (a wrong word used for its sound rather than meaning) or a repeated but unclear/misused term.
proposals.rationale: R38 contains a plain word-choice slip ('his mouth and threat were bone dry' for 'throat'). R31 repeats the unusual word 'flosculation' several times in ways that never clarify what it's meant to convey, leaving the central image muddled. Both still score very high on the scorecard (R38 0.950, R31 0.807), suggesting the scorecard isn't catching these small precision failures.

proposals.name: Emotional payoff earned by prior stakes-building
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story establishes enough context, character investment, or concrete stakes before asserting a major emotional beat (a death, a danger, a revelation), such that the beat feels dramatized rather than merely announced. HIGH: by the time the emotional claim arrives, the reader has been given real material to feel it with. LOW: a large emotional claim is asserted (stated as fact) without the scene-work needed to make a reader feel its weight.
proposals.rationale: R30 announces the parents' death in the very first exchange, with zero prior characterization of the sisters or parents, and immediately undercuts it with unrelated chatter -- the tragedy is asserted, not dramatized. R24 discusses potentially world-altering stakes (reviving the dead, repeating a historical catastrophe) entirely through abstract debate with no concrete demonstration of what's actually at risk. Compare R14, which builds Mason's stakes (his precarious position in the party, his unrequited feelings) gradually through specific scene detail before any claim is made about how he feels. R30/R24 score 0.975/0.841 on the scorecard; R14 scores 0.969 with the dense model.

proposals.name: Distinctiveness of central conceit
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story's core idea offers a genuinely surprising angle, combination, or reversal on its prompt, versus executing a familiar genre convention straightforwardly with no distinguishing hook. HIGH: the central idea is one you haven't seen many times before, or combines familiar elements in an unexpected way. LOW: the premise is a stock genre setup (a quest, a diplomatic incident, a fated meeting) executed competently but without any distinguishing twist on the idea itself.
proposals.rationale: R22's premise -- a deaf demon who can only be summoned in sign language, accidentally invoked by a special-ed teacher's botched ASL -- is a genuinely novel combination of ideas. R32 renders a time-loop through the specific, unusual lens of a character losing the ability to count days. By contrast R23 and R35 are both competently executed but generic secondary-world fantasy scenes (a quest to a legendary gate; a royal betrothal negotiation) without a distinguishing conceptual hook. R22/R32 score 0.995/0.945 with the dense model; R23/R35 score 0.951/0.863 on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Imaginative reach beyond execution polish
proposals.instruction: Judge whether the story attempts a large conceptual or temporal scope (a whole civilization's logic, a philosophical idea, centuries of history) independent of how cleanly that attempt is executed at the sentence level. Score this separately from surface polish: a rough, typo-laden piece can still score high here if it is reaching for something ambitious, and a technically clean piece can score low if its scope is narrow and safe. HIGH: the piece is trying to imagine or explain something large and complex. LOW: the piece's scope is a single small, safe moment with no attempt at larger scale or idea.
proposals.rationale: R12 attempts to lay out an entire galaxy's sociology of first contact -- statistical reasoning about how life forms, categorization of species by threat/utility, historical revisionism about 21st-century predictions -- despite being a self-described first-time writer with numerous spelling errors ('aliean,' 'exestential,' 'preverbial'). R18 attempts something similarly large (a doctrinal history of interstellar first-contact policy across centuries) but with more controlled prose. Both score very high with the dense model (0.846, 0.972) despite R12's rough execution, while the scorecard rates both near the bottom (0.015, 0.149) -- suggesting the scorecard may respond mainly to sentence-level polish rather than conceptual ambition.

proposals.name: Expository voice control in non-scene modes
proposals.instruction: For stories told in an essayistic, documentary, lecture, or summary mode rather than as a dramatized scene, judge whether the exposition itself is made compelling through a distinctive narrating voice (irony, wit, escalating specificity, invented terminology used precisely), versus reading as flat informational relay with no personality behind it. HIGH: the exposition has a point of view and could not be mistaken for a neutral summary. LOW: the piece delivers information/backstory/debate in a flat, undramatized register regardless of subject matter.
proposals.rationale: R19's non-scene, essayistic recounting of a betrothal-breaking tradition is carried entirely by a witty, ironic narrating voice ('the dance of the thing,' 'ate the decorative swan'). R18's found-document format uses precise invented terminology and escalating specificity to build tension inside a report format. By contrast R24's dialogue-driven exposition about the ethics of reviving the dead reads as flat argumentative back-and-forth with no distinguishing narratorial personality, and R09's scene is almost entirely undramatized information exchange. R19/R18 score 0.924/0.972 with the dense model; R24/R09 score 0.841/0.904 on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Escalation via new complications, not repetition
proposals.instruction: When a story builds comic or dramatic momentum through a series of escalating beats, judge whether each new beat introduces a qualitatively new complication (a new fact, character, or reversal) rather than simply repeating the same joke or observation at a larger magnitude. HIGH: each escalation surprises in a new way. LOW: the escalation is the same beat repeated with a bigger number or louder version of the same idea, or the piece's humor depends on a single external reference landing rather than a built sequence.
proposals.rationale: R34 escalates through genuinely different complications in sequence -- mistaken identity, dead instruments, an unexplained flash, an airplane materializing in space, an unexplained Space Force claiming the wreckage -- each beat is a new kind of surprise. Compare R25, whose comedy escalates only by increasing the same number (a hundred tabs, a thousand tabs, ten thousand tabs) without a qualitatively new complication, and R08, whose humor depends almost entirely on a single external topical reference landing at the very end rather than a built sequence of surprises. R34 scores 0.998 with the dense model; R25 and R08 score 0.982 and 0.948 on the scorecard.

proposals.name: Earned dramatic irony: reader sees past the narrator
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the text lets the reader assemble something the narrator does not state or does not grasp -- the narrator's identity, species, situation, or self-deception -- and the story's effect depends on that gap being crossed by the reader. Score 3 when a mild gap exists but the story also spells it out. Score 1 when narrator knowledge and reader knowledge are identical throughout, so every fact arrives as direct statement and there is nothing to infer. Do not credit mere vagueness or withheld information that is never recoverable; the reader must be able to close the gap from the shown text.
proposals.rationale: R20 never says the narrator is a dog or that the dying 'Great-Long-Lived' is a human owner, yet the offerings, the 'One-of-Nine', and the paw laid in comfort make it unmistakable. R32's narrator explains away his own transformation while the reader watches it finish ('her unhinged jaw melding with mine'); R05's narrator recounts interbreeding-or-extermination as routine housekeeping. All three are dense_high_card_low. The card-high rows run the other way: R01 and R15 announce their premises and then illustrate them, leaving the reader no work.

proposals.name: Invented specifics implying a system offstage
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the story supplies proper nouns, customs, terminology, institutions, or economics that the prompt did not provide, uses them as if they were ordinary, and keeps them internally consistent. Score 1 when everything in the story was already implied by the prompt line and the nouns are generic placeholders ('the Rider', 'the Orb', 'the creature'). Judge invention, not word count: one well-placed invented custom outranks a paragraph of adjectives.
proposals.rationale: R19 invents the War of Too Many Uncles, the House of Many Mirrors, and the peasant poet Alric Turnip (replaced at his own wedding by a trained ferret); R30 invents the doctrine of 'first exposure-first extinction' and the Echlmaar'ch of Gliese 674; R09 invents an occupational economy in which the terror's head is scalped and carved into a new hilt. All are card-low and dense-high. By contrast card-high R12 offers only 'the Orb' and never even names the argument the two humans made, and R21 adds nothing its prompt did not already contain.

proposals.name: Prompt enacted through consequence, not recited
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the prompt's proposition is demonstrated by events and their costs, such that the story would still work if the prompt's sentence were never spoken aloud in it. Score 1 when the prompt's sentence (or a close paraphrase) is itself the payoff, or when the story is a tableau of the prompt plus backstory explaining how the tableau came about. Restating the prompt early as a scene-setter is neutral; restating it as the climax is the low end.
proposals.rationale: R05 never states the prompt's three questions and instead enacts them, ending on humanity having 'either interbred with, or eliminated these near peer alien races' -- dense .846 against card .015. R13 (card .950) spends its whole length arriving at the prompt line delivered verbatim as its final words, and R01 (card .951) stages the prompt's image and then explains the journey that produced it. The card appears to treat prompt-fidelity as satisfied by quotation.

proposals.name: Irreversible cost, judged together with surface polish
proposals.instruction: Composite. First ask whether, by the last line, something has been spent, broken, chosen, or foreclosed that cannot be taken back. Then ask whether the prose is clean and correct. Score 5 for irreversibility (clean or rough). Score 1 for the specific combination of competent, error-free prose with nothing lost -- every option still open, nobody down anything, the situation restorable. This combination is a 1, not a 3: polish is not a substitute for cost.
proposals.rationale: R14 (card .128) turns on a single committing act -- 'I answer the phone'; R26 (card .056) has the billionaire slide out of his skin; R12 (card .050) strips a species of speech permanently. Against these, card-high R01 ends with the pair merely beginning their descent, R31 (card .807) ends with the ferret asleep and the foreclosure notices still on the floor, and R06 (card .987, the slice's highest) ends a meeting after which nothing about anyone's position has changed. Clean prose with no cost is exactly the card's over-credit.

proposals.name: Fiction kept clear of frame and housekeeping material
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the fictional text runs unbroken from first word to last, and any note, plug, word count, or contest talk sits after a clear terminal line. Score 1 when such material opens the piece, interrupts it, or annotates the fiction from inside it. Position is what is scored, not presence: a trailing signature after a finished ending is not a defect; a preface or an in-body aside is.
proposals.rationale: R06 opens with an off-topic writer's note about the picture before a word of story; R36 opens by explaining its own construction ('I actually wrote two stories for this prompt') and then reprints a paragraph verbatim across the seam; R22 breaks its own conceit to comment on it ('(in the real world, there would probably be more emoji)'); R31 closes by soliciting critique. All four are card-high and dense-low, which suggests the card counts frame material as neutral trailing matter wherever it appears, while dense-high rows such as R20 and R30 keep the fiction sealed.

proposals.name: Self-contained: no borrowed affect from outside the text
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when all emotional weight is generated inside the shown text, so a reader with no outside knowledge gets the full effect. Score 1 when the story leans on an existing franchise, an earlier installment, or thread context to supply the feeling or the recognition, and a reader lacking that context loses the point. Note the exception: if the prompt itself names the borrowed material, borrowing is licensed and only the failure to add anything to it counts against the story.
proposals.rationale: R04 (card .904) imports Astro Boy wholesale -- Dr. Tenma, Tobio, the resurrected son -- and lets that history do the grieving. R33 (card .841) is Chapter 6, opening with links to previous chapters and turning on Sjorn, the Peacekeeper War, and Dragon, none of which the shown text establishes. R39 (card .980) rests its irony entirely on the reader's prior Freddy Krueger. Compare dense-high R35 and R20, which build their premises from nothing.

proposals.name: Dialogue that changes the state of play
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when each speech alters the balance between speakers -- a concession, a threat, a reversal, a cornering -- and no character tells another what both already know. Score 1 when dialogue exists to deliver background to the reader, or is banter that leaves both parties exactly where they started. The diagnostic for the low end: could the line be cut and replaced by narration without losing anything but information?
proposals.rationale: R04's characters brief each other on shared history ('I must thank you again for enlightening me upon the subject of capturing human souls'); R34's two aliens explain galactic statute to one another; R01 halts its scene to deliver centuries of cosmology. All three are card-high (.904/.948/.951). R18 is the counter-case at card .101: every line moves an argument, and the student's final question genuinely corners the professor, who has to defer it to a later lecture.

proposals.name: Form choice is load-bearing
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the piece's chosen format -- log, document, script, verse, transcript -- does work that plain narration could not: it paces, withholds, ironizes, or constrains what can be shown. Score 1 when the format is decoration that could be stripped without loss, or when the author explains the format's effect rather than letting it operate.
proposals.rationale: R08 (card .115) uses timestamps for pacing and the gaps between them for dread ('19:23 ... 19:26 Did we lose them?'), and the log form is precisely what makes the final Space Force entry land as an intrusion. R30 (card .149) makes its whole joke out of framing humanity as an entry in an alien survival manual. R26 (card .056) uses doggerel to deflate a first-contact catastrophe into a ten-quid bet. Against: card-high R22 adopts a chat transcript and then explains it, and R37 (card .876) uses lone '.' lines as spacers that carry nothing.

proposals.name: Unsubstitutable narrating voice
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the narration has a consistent idiolect -- diction, rhythm, characteristic evasions or refrains -- that could not be transplanted into another story without carrying the character with it. Score 1 for competent neutral narration that any story in the genre could share. Score voice consistency, not grammatical correctness: sustained non-standard usage that characterizes the speaker scores high; correct but anonymous prose scores low.
proposals.rationale: R20's liturgical refrain and coined vocabulary ('To serve is the highest honour', 'the Field After'), R19's mock-antiquarian cadence, R11's self-interrupting shrug ('So, even if it's weird ... who cares? I live in a mansion. Yep, I jinxed myself.'), and R10's confessional register are all dense-high and card-low (.152/.032/.152/.055), several of them with visible grammatical slips. R01, R27, and R06 narrate in interchangeable clean genre prose and are the card's top-rated rows in the slice.

proposals.name: Precise diction: unusual words earn their place
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when rare or elevated words are used correctly and the register they establish is sustained across the whole piece, and when any quotation or borrowed line is naturalized to the speaker. Score 1 when showy vocabulary is misused, or when quotations are dropped in unassimilated, or when the register lurches without motivation. Judge accuracy and consistency of vocabulary, not its difficulty.
proposals.rationale: R31 uses 'flosculation' correctly for flowery language and then again, incorrectly, for the contents of a paint jar, and has its painter recite Twain and Cicero at a ferret ('Get your facts first, then you can distort them as you please'). It is the lowest dense row in the slice at .014 yet scores card .807. R19 sustains an entire mock-historical register without a slip and scores card .032. The pair suggests the card rewards vocabulary level while missing vocabulary accuracy.

proposals.name: Consequence lands on one individuated creature
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the cost of the story is borne by a specific, individuated character whose loss is shown in behavior or sensation on the page. Score 1 when consequences are attributed to species, institutions, populations, or civilizations, so that nothing is felt by anyone in particular. A named character is not sufficient; the character must be the one who pays.
proposals.rationale: R20 (card .116) narrows a millennia-old symbiosis to one animal lying beside one failing body until 'the only heat was my own'. R07 (card .101) puts an entire isekai economy onto Mason scraping crystals off a disintegrating corpse while his friend's laughter rings behind him. Both dense-high. Card-high R34 (.948) settles galactic accounts with no one hurt on the page, and R01 (.951) pitches its stakes at 'humanity' and 'the Tree of Life' in the abstract.

proposals.name: The story refuses to gloss itself
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the emotional point and the joke are both left for the reader to complete, so the last line performs rather than summarizes. Score 1 when the text states its own meaning, names the feeling it has just produced, or explains its own punchline. Ignore whether the meaning is obvious; score only whether the story says it out loud.
proposals.rationale: R38 (card .980) delivers a three-line joke and then explains it -- 'Then he realized that he's supposed to write a fiction, not an autobiography'. R22 (card .934) annotates its own conceit mid-text. R01 (card .951) names its own ending for the reader: 'there was a sense of hope that they were all too afraid would be false'. Against these, dense-high R07 never says Mason is jealous or dependent and R20 never says grief; both leave the naming to the reader.

proposals.name: Ending closes the scene and opens the world
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the final move settles the immediate situation and simultaneously enlarges what is at stake, so the reader leaves with a larger question than they arrived with. Score 1 for either of two failure modes: nothing closes at all (the piece stops at the threshold of the story it was about to tell), or the piece is wholly exhausted by a single gag with nothing left standing after it.
proposals.rationale: R17 (card .104) resolves Cora's search through the server room and then reframes the entire war with five words on a screen; R32 (card .172) finishes the debrief and reveals the narrator has become what he killed; R08 (card .115) ends the log by opening a time bubble and an unrecorded Space Force. All dense-high. Both card-high failure modes appear in the slice: R01 (.951) ends as the journey begins, and R21 (.975) and R38 (.980) end the instant their single joke is delivered.

proposals.name: Earned idea payoff from the premise
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the story works out a genuine implication of its own premise that the reader was not handed -- a mechanism, a paradox, a social logic, an inverted consequence -- and the working-out is legible in the text. Score 1 when the premise is illustrated but never interrogated, so the story ends knowing exactly what it knew at the start.
proposals.rationale: R18 (card .101) turns the thought experiment on itself: if the Geiger counter is not a quantum entity, the box self-measures, and the professor must defer the objection. R19 (card .032) derives the self-sustaining economics of a corrupt custom -- 'The more they resent it, the more they participate, because hope ... demands investment'. R30 (card .149) inverts its own deterrence rule so that broadcasting loudly becomes armor. All three are dense-high. Card-high R27 (.891) and R34 (.948) illustrate their premises and stop.

proposals.name: Comic payoff from a planted detail, not restated premise
proposals.instruction: Score 5 when the laugh or the turn arrives on something the story quietly planted earlier -- a bystander, an object, a habit, a piece of terminology -- so that closer reading is rewarded. Score 1 when the humor is the prompt's premise restated, or a single gag announced early and simply held to the end. If the story is not comic, score whether its final turn is prepared by planted material rather than introduced fresh.
proposals.rationale: R26 (card .056) ends on 'Dave handed Tom 10 quid', retroactively installing two bored onlookers and a wager under a first-contact catastrophe. R08 (card .115) plants an unexplained flash and a drifting object before the Malaysian airliner and the Space Force captain arrive to close the 'time bubble'. R35 (card .128) sets up Demon Sign Language early and detonates it on a substitute teacher's mangled ASL. All dense-high. Card-high R21 (.975) states its joke -- a stoner cannot distinguish a hallucination from a blinking statue -- at the start and again at the end, and R34 (.948) rides one topical hair gag.

proposals.name: Causal Premise Integration
proposals.instruction: Score high when the prompt’s central premise actively causes the characters’ choices, complications, and ending; score low when it is merely mentioned or used as a thin setup.
proposals.rationale: R23 and R40 turn their premises into the engine of the plot, whereas R13 and R30 largely stop at a premise or introductory gesture.

proposals.name: Escalating Consequences
proposals.instruction: Score high when each major beat creates a sharper danger, dilemma, or complication; score low when events remain static, repetitive, or end before meaningful escalation.
proposals.rationale: R04, R23, and R35 progressively intensify their situations, while R03 and R13 provide little consequential development.

proposals.name: Earned Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score high when the ending delivers a consequence or reversal prepared by earlier details and changes the reader’s understanding; score low when it is arbitrary, merely announced, or absent.
proposals.rationale: R19, R23, and R31 plant details that pay off later, unlike the underdeveloped conclusions of R16 and R30.

proposals.name: Consequential Character Agency
proposals.instruction: Score high when characters make difficult, consequential choices that reveal priorities and alter events; score low when they mainly observe, explain, or are carried along by the plot.
proposals.rationale: R04, R37, and R40 give protagonists meaningful choices under pressure, while R16 and R30 contain comparatively passive central figures.

proposals.name: Psychological Contradiction
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character’s conflicting desires, beliefs, or self-justifications are dramatized and evolve; score low when motivation is one-note or simply stated.
proposals.rationale: R18 and R27 show characters negotiating loyalty, resentment, and obligation, while R12 and R13 offer much thinner inner movement.

proposals.name: Embodied Scene Presence
proposals.instruction: Score high when setting and emotion are conveyed through specific sensory perceptions, physical behavior, and concrete objects; score low when the story relies mainly on summary or abstract explanation.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R19 make their threats physically palpable, whereas R11 and R25 spend much of their space explaining ideas and background.

proposals.name: Coherent World Implications
proposals.instruction: Score high when unusual rules, institutions, or technologies have specific, consistent consequences visible in daily behavior; score low when worldbuilding is generic, contradictory, or presented as detached exposition.
proposals.rationale: R18, R20, and R24 infer functioning societies from their speculative rules, while R11 and R25 mostly state broad world premises.

proposals.name: Distinctive Narrative Voice
proposals.instruction: Score high when diction, rhythm, attitude, and figurative language create a recognizable narrator suited to the story; score low when the prose sounds generic, unstable, or interchangeable.
proposals.rationale: R18, R21, and R40 sustain highly recognizable voices, in contrast with the flatter explanatory narration in R11 and R25.

proposals.name: Subtextual Dialogue
proposals.instruction: Score high when dialogue reveals status, history, conflict, or personality beyond its literal information; score low when speakers merely exchange exposition or interchangeable statements.
proposals.rationale: R06, R10, and R31 use conversation to expose relationships and character, whereas R03 and R13 have deliberately thin exchanges with little subtext.

proposals.name: Tonal Control
proposals.instruction: Score high when humor, horror, sentiment, or absurdity are balanced deliberately and shifts reinforce the story’s premise; score low when tonal changes feel accidental or undermine the emotional effect.
proposals.rationale: R06, R19, and R35 coordinate comic and disturbing material, while R03 and R25 shift into jokes without comparable emotional or structural control.

proposals.name: Form as Storytelling
proposals.instruction: Score high when the chosen format—log, chat, poem, transcript, or other form—controls information and creates effects unavailable in ordinary narration; score low when formatting is merely cosmetic.
proposals.rationale: R02, R15, and R23 use constrained formats to regulate revelation and pacing, while R03’s chat format contributes little beyond surface presentation.

proposals.name: Motif Development
proposals.instruction: Score high when a repeated image, phrase, or object accumulates meaning or changes significance across the story; score low when repetition is decorative or absent.
proposals.rationale: R18’s repeated service language and R39’s recurring stars and light deepen their themes, unlike the largely non-developing imagery in R13 and R16.

proposals.name: Economy of Explanation
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story conveys necessary context through selected details and lets readers infer the rest; score low when it pauses for redundant exposition, technical listing, or explanation that the scene does not need.
proposals.rationale: R14, R23, and R39 achieve substantial effect with compressed presentation, whereas R11, R17, and R25 frequently explain their worlds directly.

proposals.name: Coherent Conceptual Surprise
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story introduces an unexpected idea or reversal that feels both fresh and logically compatible with its established world; score low when the surprise is predictable, random, or dependent on a stock joke.
proposals.rationale: R19, R21, and R40 develop unusual combinations with internal logic, while R13 and R25 rely on comparatively obvious punchlines.

proposals.name: Thematic Aftereffect
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story’s events illuminate a broader human concern—such as grief, loyalty, power, identity, or complicity—and leave that implication active after the ending; score low when the conceit ends without resonance beyond its immediate gag or event.
proposals.rationale: R18, R19, and R40 extend their premises into reflections on devotion, contamination, and social power, whereas R03 and R13 largely conclude at the joke itself.

proposals.name: Premise Reframing
proposals.instruction: Score high when the story discovers a non-obvious consequence or angle within the prompt and builds around it; score low when it merely restates the setup or adds a generic event.
proposals.rationale: R14 turns a deaf demon into a character whose summoning depends on sign language, while R40 makes human saliva an alien biological weapon. Both show deeper premise transformation than the more literal treatments in R02 and R06.

proposals.name: Distinctive Voice
proposals.instruction: Score high when diction, rhythm, attitude, and syntax create a memorable narrator or storytelling personality that remains controlled; score low when the prose sounds generic, interchangeable, or inconsistently voiced.
proposals.rationale: R10 sustains an arch satirical voice, and R36 maintains a solemn canine-religious voice. By contrast, R07 and R31 use thin, interchangeable conversational narration despite satisfying their prompts.

proposals.name: Character Agency Under Pressure
proposals.instruction: Score high when a character pursues a specific desire, makes consequential choices, and accepts meaningful costs; score low when characters mainly observe, explain, or passively undergo events.
proposals.rationale: R03 makes the father choose to confront the gang, while R38 gives Mason active decisions amid resentment and danger. R02 and R08 rely more heavily on characters explaining their situations than changing them.

proposals.name: Implied Meaning and Subtext
proposals.instruction: Score high when important emotional or thematic meaning emerges through behavior, imagery, omission, or contradiction for the judge to infer; score low when the story states its meaning directly or supplies no deeper implication.
proposals.rationale: R03 conveys the father’s concealed history through weariness, reassurance, and action, while R36 lets ritual language imply grief and dependence. R06 and R31 explain their central ideas with little subtextual work.

proposals.name: Causal Escalation
proposals.instruction: Score high when each major beat changes the characters’ options and increases pressure toward a consequential climax; score low when events remain static, arrive abruptly, or merely accumulate without changing the situation.
proposals.rationale: R30 escalates from an impossible transmission to a temporal military intervention, and R39 progressively converts confusion into imminent bodily danger. R02 and R06 mostly sustain exposition without comparable escalating choices.

proposals.name: Recontextualizing Ending
proposals.instruction: Score high when the final beat makes earlier details newly significant and feels prepared by the story; score low when the ending simply stops, states the premise again, or adds an unsupported twist.
proposals.rationale: R13’s return to the bed transforms the apparent conversation into a recurring containment system, while R40’s final encounter reframes the narrator’s infection and appetite. R18 and R28 provide premises and continuation without an equally integrated final recontextualization.

proposals.name: Form That Serves Content
proposals.instruction: Score high when the chosen form—poem, log, transcript, dialogue, or other structure—creates meaning, pacing, or limitations essential to the story; score low when formatting is merely decorative or the form could be removed without loss.
proposals.rationale: R09 uses compressed verse to enact bodily and technological transformation, R30 uses a communication log to control revelation, and R37 uses dialogue to embody a conceptual dispute. These formal choices add value beyond ordinary narration.

proposals.name: Multi-Function Concrete Detail
proposals.instruction: Score high when specific physical details simultaneously establish character or setting, shape tone, and foreshadow or complicate events; score low when details are vague, ornamental, or presented as unconnected lists.
proposals.rationale: R11’s smell, blade, dream-edge, and melting terror establish both method and atmosphere, while R36’s domestic sensations carry the alien canine perspective and grief. R12 and R18 contain many descriptive details that are less tightly functional.

proposals.name: World Rules Through Consequences
proposals.instruction: Score high when speculative rules become clear through what characters do, suffer, or risk; score low when the story pauses for encyclopedia-like explanation or introduces mechanics without observable consequences.
proposals.rationale: R27 reveals interstellar doctrine through civilizations’ strategic behavior, and R40 explains alien biology through injury and transformation. R02 and R06 state extensive world history and rules directly, which can appear complete while remaining dramatically inert.

proposals.name: Productive Ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Score high when uncertainty supports multiple plausible interpretations anchored by textual clues and increases tension or meaning; score low when ambiguity results mainly from omitted information, inconsistency, or arbitrary withholding.
proposals.rationale: R13 leaves the nature of Cherry’s world uncertain while supplying recurring behavioral clues, and R28 keeps the mansion’s agency and the narrator’s immunity intriguingly unresolved. Their ambiguity differs from simple incompleteness in R02 and R32.

proposals.name: Controlled Tonal Collision
proposals.instruction: Score high when humor, horror, absurdity, or earnestness collide through deliberate transitions that deepen the scene; score low when jokes, sentiment, or genre shifts randomly weaken the stakes.
proposals.rationale: R10’s bureaucratic romantic satire and R14’s grotesque demon comedy sustain intentional tonal tension. R35 also uses comic authorial cruelty effectively, unlike stories where incidental jokes interrupt rather than reshape the dramatic mood.

proposals.name: Earned Emotional Resonance
proposals.instruction: Score high when emotion grows from a specific relationship, vulnerability, or loss and changes the character’s behavior; score low when reactions are generic, melodramatic, or unsupported by prior attachment.
proposals.rationale: R36 grounds grief in years of reciprocal care between the animal guard and its human, while R03 grounds courage in a father-son bond. R08 and R22 name strong relationships and loss but provide less accumulated emotional evidence.

proposals.name: Moral Complexity
proposals.instruction: Score high when the premise creates competing, intelligible values or obligations and the story resists an easy moral verdict; score low when morality is reduced to obvious heroes, villains, or an asserted lesson.
proposals.rationale: R04 complicates humanity’s response to alien life by making humans both threatened and destructive, while R38 complicates survival, dependency, and moral numbness. R06 and R17 resolve their ethical premises more mechanically.

proposals.name: Compression Without Dead Weight
proposals.instruction: Score high when nearly every sentence advances plot, characterization, atmosphere, voice, or interpretation; score low when the story repeats information, digresses, front-loads exposition, or includes distracting author commentary.
proposals.rationale: R09 achieves a complete reversal in very few lines, and R19 compresses disorientation and renewed agency into a tightly patterned monologue. R02 and R31 spend substantial space on setup or self-description without equivalent narrative movement.

proposals.name: Dynamic Power in Relationships
proposals.instruction: Score high when dialogue and action reveal changing leverage, mismatched knowledge, dependence, affection, or threat between characters; score low when interactions merely exchange exposition and leave the relationships unchanged.
proposals.rationale: R14 shifts Tyler from neglected outcast to terrifying controller, while R38 exposes Mason’s dependence and resentment through his interactions with Kale and Zell. R06 and R23 have conversational exchanges that explain circumstances but produce fewer relational reversals.
